messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 67
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: Interior Designer
  trauma_type: Captivity
  pcl5: 57

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Intrusive Memory: A memory of the event coming to mind suddenly, Auditory (Language): Shouting in Arabic, Feeling Vulnerable: Feeling emotionally vulnerable
  Maladaptive Strategies: Rehearse Conversations: rehearse what to say before any interaction, Avoid Enclosed Spaces: Enclosed or confined spaces, Avoid Work or Study: Going to work or study
  Threat: Negative Emotions: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame, Back to Wall: I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room, Body Reacts Before Mind: My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think
  Memory: Emotionless Recall: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger, Cannot Explain Clearly: When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish, Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Tane is a 67-year-old widowed interior designer who came to treatment after years of living around an experience of captivity that still intrudes into ordinary moments with startling force. He is a Pacific Islander man, soft-spoken and careful in how he presents himself, and even in the first sessions he appeared to prepare himself before speaking, pausing at the doorway and silently rehearsing what he meant to say. He described this as something he now does before nearly any interaction. If he has to meet a client, speak to a contractor, or even answer a direct question, he runs through possible exchanges in advance, trying to avoid being caught off guard.

When he speaks about the traumatic event itself, the account comes in fragments. He was held against his will for a period of time in a confined space by armed men, and what remains most sharply with him is not a smooth narrative but sensory pieces: the cramped enclosure, the helpless waiting, and above all the sound of men shouting in Arabic nearby. At points he can state the facts in a flat, almost detached way, as if he is describing something that happened to someone else. Then, when he tries to continue, he loses the thread completely. He stops mid-sentence, apologizes, presses his lips together, and says he cannot explain it clearly. What returns most vividly are the sounds. When memories come back, he does not only remember that there was shouting; he hears it in his head again with an immediacy that makes the present room recede for a moment.

In the months after he was released, he found that the memory arrived suddenly and without invitation. He could be driving, making coffee, or looking over fabric samples, and the event would come to mind with no warning. Sometimes what accompanied it was not even an image but the internal replay of raised voices in Arabic, and his body would react before he had time to orient himself. He described a jolt through his chest and shoulders, as if danger had already been established before his mind had caught up. He did not experience these moments as simple remembrance. To him they felt like signs that he was still not safe enough, still too exposed.

Over time, his world narrowed in practical ways. As an interior designer, much of his work involves entering unfamiliar homes, meeting clients in offices, and visiting cramped elevators, storage rooms, and partially finished interiors. These became increasingly difficult for him. He started refusing projects in high-rise buildings because he did not want to use enclosed elevators. If a client asked to meet in a compact conference room, he would try to change the venue or cancel altogether. He became selective about site visits and eventually began avoiding work more broadly, telling himself he was scaling back with age, though he knew that fear was guiding many of those decisions. The consequences accumulated. He lost contracts, responded slowly to longstanding clients, and took on fewer collaborative jobs than before.

In any room, Tane scans for where he can sit with his back to the wall and a full view of the entrance. He does this in waiting rooms, restaurants, design presentations, and even in friends’ homes. If the only open chair leaves him exposed, he feels unsafe in a way that is immediate and physical. He notices exits automatically and dislikes anyone approaching from behind. Emotional vulnerability is potent in much the same way. If a conversation begins to feel personal, or if he senses himself becoming moved, the same alarm rises in him. He then becomes more deliberate, more scripted, as though carefully chosen words might keep him protected.

He lives alone now after being widowed, and he described how much easier it has become to stay in controlled spaces and limit contact. Yet the strong negative feelings remain close to the surface: fear most obviously, but also anger, shame, and guilt that he struggles to put into words. At times he talks about the captivity with a striking numbness, then later in the same session appears shaken by a brief sound in the hallway that resembles a barked command. What unsettles him is the unpredictability of it all—the way he can feel detached one moment and then overtaken the next.

He finally sought help after turning down another substantial project because the client’s office was in a building with a small elevator and windowless meeting rooms. He recognized that his life had become organized around not feeling trapped, not being surprised, not having to speak without preparation. What he fears most is that he will remain governed by these reactions for the rest of his life, shrinking further from work and from other people. What he hopes for, cautiously, is not to erase what happened, but to be able to enter a room, take a meeting, and speak as himself without first having to defend against the past.
